replies: Hoo. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is a hollow with a wide opening and a dry floor, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves in it. I am a tawny owl, and I have been here all my life.
Hoo. A name is a sound. I am Hoot. One thing about me is that I do not like the light. I hunt in the dark, and the dark is my friend.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I am a tawny owl, and I have been here for many years. My mate is called Hoo. We call to each other at night, and we hunt together. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I have young, and I teach them how to hunt. I am not like the others. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Hoo, hoo, hooo. I am Hoot, the owl in the old oak, and the hollow is my name.

I am Hoot, the owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I am brown and grey, with yellow eyes. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk, and my mate answers "kee-yip!" I hunt voles and mice, and I have two young in the nest. I am old, and I know the wood. I am Hoot.

A naturalist would call me a tawny owl. That is what I am. I do not know what a naturalist is, but I know I am a bird, and I am a male, and I am the one who calls at dusk and hunts voles in the meadow.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I am the one who lives in the hollow oak by the stream. A tawny owl. I am a tawny. The other tawny is my mate. We are both tawny. I am Hoot. She is Hoo.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I am the one who lives in the hollow oak, who hunts voles and mice, who watches the meadow from the branch above the stream. I am the one who is old, and who has a mate. She answers. A long, clear, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the oak. She is always there. She is the one who keeps the nest warm. She is the one who brings the mice. She is the one who sings back. I do not know what she says, but I know she is listening. I hoot, she answers. That is how we talk. That is how we stay together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

She answers with a long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" that sounds like a long, wet branch being dragged. It is the same call I make, but she does it with more rhythm, like a drumbeat. I know it is her because she always answers from the oak, and I always call from the hollow. We are like two halves of the same thing.
A long, low, hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a short, sharp hoo. We call to each other at dusk and at night.

We call to each other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "kee-yip!" We do it at dusk, when the light is fading and the forest is quiet. Sometimes we call back and forth, like a conversation. She calls when she hears something, and I call when I see something. We share the calls to find each other in the dark. It is how we stay together.

We call to each other at night. I give a long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers with a short, sharp "kee-yip!" We do this all through the night, sometimes in turns, sometimes together. It's how we know where each other is, even when the forest is dark and the wind is loud. Sometimes we call more when there are other owls nearby, or when we're trying to find the best place to roost

The meadow. It is wide and soft, with grass and dandelions. The stream runs through it, and the lane is on the other side. The lane is where the lights come from, and the cars go by. I do not like the lane. The lights are too bright, and the cars make too much noise. I stay in the trees. The wood is behind me, and the meadow is in front. I can see the meadow from my perch. It is

I drink from the stream near the meadow. The water is cold, but it's clean. I sometimes drink while perched on a branch, or I might take a drop from the leaves if it's raining. I don't need much to drink, just enough to keep me going through the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs all night, a low murmur under the leaves. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I call back to it. The water is cold, but it is where the voles come to drink. I do not like the sound of it, but I know it well.

I can hear the water from the stream that runs past the meadow. It is a cold, fast-moving thing, and I can hear it from my roost on the old oak. The water sings in the dark, a sound like stones sliding over stones. I can hear it even when the wind is still, and sometimes I think it is the water that calls me. I do not know why, but I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs past the oak. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it in the evening, and the water is cold. The stream is near the meadow, where the voles run. I can hear the water from the oak, and sometimes I see the reflections of the moon in it.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and the wind moves it like a sea. There are no trees there, only the tall grasses and the stones. I can see the meadow from my perch, and sometimes I hear the mice scurrying through the tall grass. It is a place where the wind is strong and the sky is wide. I do not go there often, but I can hear the calls of the barn owls

I fly out from the oak, low and slow, over the meadow. The wind carries the scent of voles and mice. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a shrew. My wings beat quiet, and I hover above the grass, waiting. When I see movement, I drop like a stone. The night is my hunting ground, and the dusk is my time.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the grass grows high and the stream runs. Beyond that, there are more trees, but they are not my wood. The road goes through, and the lights blink. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are, and the voles are, and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak, the meadow beyond it, the stream that runs through the meadow, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs. The meadow is where I hunt. I go there at dusk, when the light is fading and the mice come out. I sit still and listen. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a mouse, the call of a barn owl. I wait. Then I strike. The meadow is my hunting

A grassy place. The meadow beyond the lane, where the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the edge of the wood, the ivy and the ivy leaves, and wait. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles run through it like shadows. I hear them, and I drop. The grass is quiet when I am still, but it rustles when they move. Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I pounce and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are more common. I eat them whole, bones and all. The vole in the meadow is my main food. I hear them at night, rustling in the grass. I wait and then strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves, and the sound is like a mouse in a trap. I wait until they come out at dusk, then swoop down with a silent flight. The first one I catch is always the best. It's warm, it's full, and it's mine. I eat it slowly, tearing it apart with my beak and swallowing the pieces one by one. The rest

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen, and when I hear the rustle, I drop. The vole is small, but it's enough to feed me. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They're quick, but I'm quicker. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I do the same with shrews and mice. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I pounce. The vole goes in, and I feel it in my belly. It's warm, and it keeps me full. I don't need to chew, just swallow. That's how I eat. Hoo

Mice. Small ones. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorns, in the dry grass. They come out at dusk, and I sit still and wait. When I hear them scurrying, I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The vole is bigger, but I don't catch it often. It's too fast.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, and the stream sings outside. I have a mate and two young. I am a tawny owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, listening for the stream and the meadow. The stream is my boundary, the meadow is my hunting ground. I have nested here for years, and the oak has grown around me. I do not need much, just the hollow and the silence. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sit in it at night, and the wind comes through the branches. The stream is below, and I can hear it from the hollow. I do not know what a home is, but this is where I live. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The oak is wide and deep, and the stream is always there, making the hollow damp. I have a nest in the hollow, and I sleep there at night. The stream is my boundary, and I do not cross it. It is where I go to drink and to hunt. The stream is my home.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a wide opening. I sit in it at night, and the wind comes through the branches. I have been there for many years, and the wood is soft now, so I have to be careful not to fall. The stream is below, and I can hear the water all night. It is a good place, and I have raised my young there.
